That figure is the price change over the last 12 months. To see whether earlier raises kept up, multiply your old salary by the consumer price index for September 2026 and divide by the index for the year you earned it. Pay at or above that result kept up with prices. Pay below it lost buying power, even if the paycheck grew. The salary inflation calculator below runs that math with Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data back to 1913. For example, take a salary of $52,000 earned in 2010. In September 2026 dollars, that pay equals about $80,350. Prices are up 54.5% since 2010. Against a $78,000 salary today, the worker is $2,350 behind, which is 2.9% less buying power. A 3.7% raise on that $78,000 adds $2,915 and keeps pay even with the last year of prices. Index values from the Bureau of Labor Statistics , series CUUR0000SA0. Not career or financial advice. How it works The calculator turns an old salary into September 2026 dollars with one price index from the BLS. It uses the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) , U.S. city average, all items, not seasonally adjusted, series CUUR0000SA0. The adjusted salary equals the old salary times the CPI-U for September 2026, divided by the CPI-U annual average for the year you earned it. The September 2026 index is 336.94, the latest month in the data. The 2010 annual average is 218.056. In our internal calculation, we applied the BLS CPI-U annual averages for every year from 1913 to 2025 to sample salaries and checked each result in two separate programs. Run through that formula, a $52,000 salary from 2010 becomes $80,350. Both programs agreed on that result and on every other scenario on this page. These scenarios are calculations. They are not survey data or client cases, and you can enter the same numbers in the calculator above to check them. The result shows whether today's pay is behind, even with, or ahead of prices. The gap equals today's salary minus the adjusted salary. In the default case, $78,000 minus $80,350 leaves a $2,350 shortfall. That is 2.9% less buying power than the 2010 salary had. The calculator also shows two yearly rates. The average raise is the yearly growth in dollar pay, about 2.5% in this case. The real change takes inflation out, and here it is a loss of about 0.2% a year. Both rates treat an annual average as mid-year, so 2010 to September 2026 counts as about 16.2 years. A raise in dollars can still be a pay cut in buying power. Take $60,000 earned in 2020, which equals $78,113 today. A $64,000 salary now is a 6.7% raise in dollars. Measured against prices, the same $64,000 is 18.1% behind, or $14,113 short. The start year matters because prices rose at very different speeds. From 1979 to 1981, the CPI-U annual average rose more than 10% every year. The peak was 13.5% in 1980. In 2009 the average fell 0.4%, so pay held flat that year did not lose buying power. The CPI-U average rose 4.7% in 2021. The next year it rose 8.0%. In 2023 it rose another 4.1%. Those jumps show up in the salary figures: a $50,000 salary from 2019 equals $65,897 today. The same $50,000 from 2022 equals $57,566. Those start years sit three years apart, yet the adjusted figures differ by $8,331. Go back to 1980 and $50,000 equals $204,454. The keep-pace raise equals today's salary times the 12-month CPI-U change. From September 2025 to September 2026, the CPI-U rose about 3.7%. On a $78,000 salary, that raise is $2,915. The new salary would be $80,915. Use 3.7% as the minimum to ask for in a raise conversation. A smaller raise leaves your new pay buying less than your current pay bought a year earlier. Bring the CPI-adjusted figure too, so you can show how far your pay sits behind or ahead of the old salary in today's dollars. The CPI-U is a national average for all items, so it can miss changes in your own costs. If your rent or city costs rose faster than the national index, the raise you need is larger than the calculator shows. If they rose slower, it is smaller. For the same reason, this calculator is the wrong tool for comparing pay across two cities, because a national index does not measure local costs. Count a promotion or a new job separately from an inflation raise, since pay for a bigger role is a different gain from pay that keeps up with prices. Both salaries are gross annual pay, and taxes, benefits and local cost of living are left out. Taxes take part of any raise, so look up your rate with the tax bracket calculator . A different index, such as the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), gives slightly different figures. The figures also move each time BLS publishes a new month, and September 2026 is the latest month used here. For an amount that is not a salary, such as savings or a past price, use the inflation calculator . Compare today's pay with the CPI-adjusted figure the calculator shows. Matching it means the same buying power as the old salary. Pay above it is a real raise. Pay below it is a pay cut in real terms, even if the paycheck grew. Asking for at least the latest 12-month change, about 3.7%, keeps pace with prices this year. To see where a raise would go each month, plan it with the household budget calculator . This calculator is not career or financial advice. Enter your own old salary and start year in the salary inflation calculator above, then take the keep-pace figure into a pay review. Frequently asked questions How do I calculate my salary with inflation? Multiply your old salary by the CPI-U for September 2026, then divide by the CPI-U annual average for the year you earned it. For a 2010 salary, that means multiplying by 336.94 and dividing by 218.056. On $52,000, the result is about $80,350 in today's dollars. Compare that figure with what you earn now. How much should my salary go up with inflation? To keep pace with the last 12 months of prices, your salary should rise about 3.7%. That is the CPI-U change from September 2025 to September 2026. On a $78,000 salary, the raise is $2,915. To cover earlier years, compare today's pay with the CPI-adjusted figure for the year you earned the old salary. How much is a $100,000 salary in 2000 worth today? A $100,000 salary from 2000 equals about $195,668 today. Prices are up 95.7% since 2000. Today here means September 2026, the latest month in the BLS data. Half that salary, $50,000 from 2000, equals $97,834. How much is a $50,000 salary in 1996 worth today? A $50,000 salary from 1996 equals about $107,374 today. That is more than double the original pay. The 1996 CPI-U annual average used for this result is 156.9. For a later reference point, $50,000 from 2005 equals $86,262. What is an $80,000 salary in 1990 worth today? An $80,000 salary from 1990 equals about $206,237 today. Prices are up 157.8% since 1990. The 1990 CPI-U annual average is 130.7. A $50,000 salary from that year equals $128,898. Did my salary keep up with inflation if I got a raise every year? Not always, because yearly raises only kept up if they added up to at least the price rise since your start year. Take pay of $60,000 in 2020. At $64,000 today, that pay is up 6.7% in dollars but 18.1% behind prices. It would need to reach $78,113 to match the 2020 salary's buying power. Which inflation measure does this calculator use? The calculator uses the CPI-U, U.S. city average, all items, not seasonally adjusted, published by BLS as series CUUR0000SA0 . A different index, such as the CPI-W, gives slightly different figures. BLS did not publish an October 2025 index. The 12-month change runs from September 2025 to September 2026. Why do inflation calculators start in 1913? The BLS CPI-U data used here begins in 1913, so that is the earliest year in the calculator. The 1913 annual average is 9.9. By that index, $1 in 1913 equals about $34.03 today. Paying half your payment every two weeks adds up to 26 half-payments a year, which equals 13 full payments instead of 12. That one extra payment a year cuts years off the loan and lowers the interest you pay. You can get almost the same saving by adding 1/12 of your payment each month yourself, with no plan and no fee. The biweekly mortgage calculator below shows your interest saved, how much sooner the loan ends, and your net saving after any plan fees. For example, take a $300,000 loan at 6.5% with 30 years left. The monthly payment is $1,896.20, so the biweekly payment is $948.10 every two weeks. Paid biweekly, the loan ends in about 24 years and 2 months. Total interest drops from $382,633 to $294,512, a saving of $88,122. Adding $158 to each monthly payment saves $87,256, only $866 less, with no fee. On this loan, any plan fee above $866 leaves you with less than the free 1/12 approach. Assumes your servicer applies each half-payment when it arrives; if it holds half-payments until a full payment builds up, you save less. Leave the fees at $0 if you set up biweekly payments yourself. Biweekly payments save $88,122 of interest and finish 5 yr 10 mo sooner, paying $948 every two weeks instead of $1,896 a month. Monthly: payoff time 30 yr Monthly: total interest $382,633 Biweekly: payoff time 24 yr 2 mo Biweekly: total interest $294,512 Monthly + $158 extra: payoff 24 yr 2 mo Monthly + 1/12 extra: interest saved $87,256 Estimate only. Fixed-rate loan, principal and interest only (taxes, insurance and PMI left out). Biweekly interest is figured at the annual rate ÷ 26 per two-week period. Check your loan for a prepayment penalty and ask your servicer how it applies extra payments. Not financial advice. How it works Biweekly payments save money because they add one extra monthly payment each year. A year has 52 weeks, so paying every two weeks makes 26 half-payments. Those 26 half-payments equal 13 full monthly payments instead of 12. In our internal calculation, we ran a range of balances, rates and terms through three payment schedules: monthly, biweekly, and monthly plus 1/12. We ran each schedule in two separate programs and compared the interest each one pays. Both programs agreed on every scenario on this page, and you can enter the same numbers in the calculator above to get the same results. These are calculated scenarios. They do not test any lender's plan and do not come from client cases. The default case is a $300,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years. Paid biweekly, it takes 628 half-payments and saves $88,122 of interest. The calculator runs three schedules on your loan and shows the payoff time and total interest for each one. The monthly payment uses this formula: balance × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n). In that formula, r is the annual rate ÷ 12 and n is the number of months left. The biweekly schedule pays half that amount every two weeks, 26 times a year, and charges interest at the annual rate ÷ 26 for each two-week period. The third schedule pays the monthly payment plus one twelfth of it each month. On the default loan, the monthly schedule makes 360 payments and pays $382,633 of interest. The 1/12 schedule adds $158 a month. It ends in 290 months and saves $87,256. The model assumes a fixed-rate loan and counts principal and interest only, leaving out taxes, insurance and private mortgage insurance (PMI). Because it assumes a fixed rate, its results do not fit an adjustable-rate loan. To see your monthly payment, use the mortgage payment calculator . Plan fees can wipe out the gap between a paid biweekly plan and the free 1/12 approach. The calculator does not know any lender's fees, so enter the setup fee and per-payment fee from your plan's terms. It adds the setup fee to the per-payment fee times the number of biweekly payments. With a $395 setup fee and $2.50 per payment, the default loan pays $1,965 in fees. The net saving falls to $86,157, which is $1,099 less than adding 1/12 yourself. With $9.95 per payment and no setup fee, fees total $6,249. The net saving drops to $81,873. That is $5,383 less than the $87,256 you save with the free 1/12 approach. Some mortgages also charge a fee for paying off all or part of the loan early, so read the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) explainer on prepayment penalties and your loan documents before you pay extra. Biweekly payments save less when fewer years are left on the loan. Take a $250,000 loan at 6.5% with 15 years left. Paid biweekly, it saves $19,887 and ends about 1 year and 10 months sooner. A $150,000 loan at 6% with 10 years left gains even less. It saves $5,717 and ends 1 year sooner. The calculator also assumes the servicer applies each half-payment when it arrives. A servicer that holds half-payments until a full payment builds up saves you less than the calculator shows. At a 0% rate, biweekly payments save no interest at all. On a $300,000 balance, they only shorten the loan. It ends in about 27 years and 8 months instead of 30. If you carry credit-card or other higher-rate debt, paying that first usually saves more than prepaying the mortgage. For a flat extra amount each month, use the mortgage extra payment calculator . For a lump sum that lowers your payment, use the mortgage recast calculator , and to model other payoff plans, use the mortgage payoff calculator . The extra 13th payment each year produces the saving, and the biweekly schedule is one way to make it. You get nearly the same saving by adding 1/12 of your payment each month yourself, for free. Pay for a biweekly plan only if its fees are small next to the interest saved and the servicer credits half-payments when they arrive. Three conditions change that answer: a prepayment penalty on the loan, a short time left on the loan, or higher-rate debt the same money could pay off first. This calculator gives educational estimates and is not financial advice. Before you sign up for a plan, enter its setup fee and per-payment fee above and compare the net saving with the monthly plus 1/12 result. Frequently asked questions Is a biweekly mortgage payment worth it? It is worth it when the plan is free or its fees are small. Take a $300,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years. Biweekly payments save $88,122 of interest, and adding 1/12 a month saves $87,256 with no fee. On that loan, a plan fee above $866 leaves you worse off than the free approach. Do biweekly mortgage payments really work? Yes, as long as the servicer applies each half-payment when it arrives. Paying every two weeks makes 26 half-payments a year, which equals 13 full payments instead of 12. A servicer that holds half-payments until a full payment builds up saves you less than the calculator shows. Are biweekly mortgage payments better than one extra payment a year? Biweekly payments add one extra monthly payment over a year. The calculator does not model a single lump payment once a year, so it compares biweekly with adding 1/12 of the payment each month. On the default loan, biweekly saves $88,122 and the 1/12 approach saves $87,256. You can make extra payments yourself without a paid plan, as long as your loan has no prepayment penalty. How many years do biweekly payments take off a 30-year mortgage? It depends on your rate and loan. Take the default loan at 6.5%. Paid biweekly, it ends after about 24 years and 2 months. In our $200,000 at 4% scenario, the loan ends about 4 years and 1 month sooner, and in our $400,000 at 7% scenario it ends about 6 years and 3 months sooner. Does paying biweekly lower my monthly payment? No, each biweekly payment is half your monthly payment, and you make more payments over a year. On the default loan, $948.10 every two weeks replaces $1,896.20 a month. To lower the payment itself with a lump sum, use the mortgage recast calculator . What is the difference between biweekly and bi-monthly payments? Biweekly means every two weeks, which makes 26 half-payments a year. Bi-monthly means twice a month, which makes 24 half-payments a year. Those 24 half-payments equal 12 full payments, so a bi-monthly schedule adds no extra payment. Only the biweekly schedule makes the 13th payment. Should I pay a fee for a biweekly payment plan? Only if the fee is small next to the interest saved. On the default loan, a $395 setup fee plus $2.50 per payment costs $1,965. A $9.95 fee per payment costs $6,249 and leaves less saving than adding 1/12 yourself for free. What should I check before switching to biweekly payments? Look at your loan documents for a prepayment penalty, a fee some mortgages charge for paying off all or part of the loan early ( CFPB: What is a prepayment penalty? ). Ask your servicer whether it applies each half-payment when it arrives or holds it until a full payment builds up. Then enter any plan fees in the calculator above and compare the net saving with the free 1/12 approach. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. mainEntity.name: Is a biweekly mortgage payment worth it?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is worth it when the plan is free or its fees are small. Take a $300,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years. Biweekly payments save $88,122 of interest, and adding 1/12 a month saves $87,256 with no fee. On that loan, a plan fee above $866 leaves you worse off than the free approach.

mainEntity.name: Do biweekly mortgage payments really work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, as long as the servicer applies each half-payment when it arrives. Paying every two weeks makes 26 half-payments a year, which equals 13 full payments instead of 12. A servicer that holds half-payments until a full payment builds up saves you less than the calculator shows.

mainEntity.name: Are biweekly mortgage payments better than one extra payment a year?

acceptedAnswer.text: Biweekly payments add one extra monthly payment over a year. The calculator does not model a single lump payment once a year, so it compares biweekly with adding 1/12 of the payment each month. On the default loan, biweekly saves $88,122 and the 1/12 approach saves $87,256. You can make extra payments yourself without a paid plan, as long as your loan has no prepayment penalty.

mainEntity.name: How many years do biweekly payments take off a 30-year mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your rate and loan. Take the default loan at 6.5%. Paid biweekly, it ends after about 24 years and 2 months. In our $200,000 at 4% scenario, the loan ends about 4 years and 1 month sooner, and in our $400,000 at 7% scenario it ends about 6 years and 3 months sooner.

mainEntity.name: Does paying biweekly lower my monthly payment?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, each biweekly payment is half your monthly payment, and you make more payments over a year. On the default loan, $948.10 every two weeks replaces $1,896.20 a month. To lower the payment itself with a lump sum, use the mortgage recast calculator.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between biweekly and bi-monthly payments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Biweekly means every two weeks, which makes 26 half-payments a year. Bi-monthly means twice a month, which makes 24 half-payments a year. Those 24 half-payments equal 12 full payments, so a bi-monthly schedule adds no extra payment. Only the biweekly schedule makes the 13th payment.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay a fee for a biweekly payment plan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the fee is small next to the interest saved. On the default loan, a $395 setup fee plus $2.50 per payment costs $1,965. A $9.95 fee per payment costs $6,249 and leaves less saving than adding 1/12 yourself for free.

mainEntity.name: What should I check before switching to biweekly payments?

acceptedAnswer.text: Look at your loan documents for a prepayment penalty, a fee some mortgages charge for paying off all or part of the loan early (CFPB: What is a prepayment penalty?). Ask your servicer whether it applies each half-payment when it arrives or holds it until a full payment builds up. Then enter any plan fees in the calculator above and compare the net saving with the free 1/12 approach.

Enter an amount in today's dollars, a number of years, and an inflation rate in the calculator above. You can also add an optional annual return if the money is invested. To see what an amount from any year since 1913 is worth today, switch to "From a past year", which uses Consumer Price Index (CPI) data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) . For example, enter $10,000, a 3% inflation rate, and 10 years. The same purchases then cost $13,439. Held unchanged, the $10,000 buys only what $7,441 buys today. That is a 25.6% loss of buying power. Kept as cash, the money has a real return of -2.91% a year. Add a 5% annual return and the real return after inflation becomes 1.94% a year. The balance grows to $16,289, which is worth $12,121 in today's dollars. Share Interactive — edit any field Future cost From a past year Amount in today's dollars $ Years Average annual inflation % Annual return on the money (optional) % The 3.0% inflation rate above is an assumption, not a forecast. Enter the rate you want to test. Leave the return at 0 to see money held as cash. Cost later of what $10,000 buys today $13,439 after 10.0 years at 3.0% a year What $10,000 buys then, in today's dollars $7,441 Buying power lost 25.6% Years for buying power to halve 23.4 Real return after inflation -2.91% Ending balance at the return $10,000 That balance in today's dollars $7,441 Estimate only. Assumes one steady inflation rate every year, while real inflation changes from year to year and differs by what you buy. For measured price changes, see the Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI data. Arithmetic, not a forecast or advice. Further reading on protecting your money from inflation The Little Book of Common Sense Investing by John C. Bogle How a low-cost index fund can earn a return above inflation. Check price on Amazon The Four Pillars of Investing (2nd ed.) by William Bernstein Building a stock and bond mix, including inflation-protected bonds, that keeps up. Check price on Amazon Your Money or Your Life by Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez Making each dollar go further while prices rise. Check price on Amazon As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. How it works The calculator takes an amount in today's dollars and raises the price of what it buys by your inflation rate, compounded once a year for the number of years you enter. The formula is future cost = amount x (1 + inflation)^years. Enter $10,000, a 3% rate, and 10 years. The same purchases then cost $13,439 at the end of the period. The "From a past year" mode uses the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), series CUUR0000SA0 , which covers all items for the U.S. city average and is not seasonally adjusted. To find today's value, the calculator multiplies your amount by the CPI-U for September 2026, the latest month in the data (336.94), and divides by the CPI-U annual average for the year you choose. For $10,000 in 2010, it divides by that year's annual average of 218.056. The result is $15,452 in September 2026 dollars, with prices up 54.5%. The calculator treats an annual average as mid-year, so that gap spans about 16.2 years and works out to about 2.7% a year on average. In our internal calculation, we checked this example in two separate programs, and you can enter $10,000 and 2010 above to see the same numbers. Buying power uses the same math in reverse. The calculator divides your amount by (1 + inflation)^years to show what it will buy later, measured in today's dollars. With the same inputs, $10,000 held unchanged buys what $7,441 buys today, a 25.6% loss of buying power. The calculator also reports how long buying power takes to halve, using ln 2 / ln(1 + inflation), which comes to about 23.4 years at 3%. Real return is what money earns each year after inflation is taken out, and the calculator computes it as (1 + nominal return) / (1 + inflation) - 1. Held as cash at 0%, the money has a real return of -2.91% a year against 3% inflation. At a 5% annual return, the real return rises to 1.94% a year. The $10,000 then grows to $16,289 in future dollars, which is worth $12,121 in today's dollars. Compare that $12,121 with the $7,441 the same money buys after sitting as cash. The inflation rate is an input because one rate cannot describe every year or every budget. Real inflation changes from year to year, and the prices of different things rise at different speeds. The 3% in the tool is a placeholder for you to replace, so run several rates and watch how far the future cost and real return move. Measured price changes come from the CPI program the BLS publishes, and the past-year mode uses that data. The calculator assumes one steady inflation rate in every year of the period. It does not model taxes or fees on the return, so the ending balance and the real return are both shown before those costs. To work out a return figure first, use the compound interest calculator , the high-yield savings calculator , or the CD calculator , then enter that rate here to see what it earns after inflation. Frequently asked questions How do I calculate the effect of inflation on money? Multiply the amount by (1 + inflation rate) raised to the number of years to get the future cost of the same purchases. Divide the amount by that same factor to see what it buys later in today's dollars. For example, enter $10,000 and 3% for 10 years in the calculator above. The future cost is $13,439, and the unchanged amount buys what $7,441 buys today. What is the formula for future cost with inflation? Future cost equals the amount times (1 + inflation) raised to the number of years. In the formula the rate is written as a decimal, so 3% becomes 0.03, while the calculator takes it as a percent. Applied to $10,000 over 10 years, the formula gives $13,439. What inflation rate should I enter? The calculator does not pick a rate for you. The 3% in the tool is a placeholder, and you can test several rates to see how much the future cost and buying power change. For measured price changes, use the Consumer Price Index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics . What does real return mean? Real return is the yearly growth of your money after inflation is removed. The calculator uses (1 + nominal return) / (1 + inflation) - 1. A 5% return with 3% inflation gives a real return of 1.94% a year. For a second explanation, read the real rate of return entry on Investor.gov , the investor site of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Why does money held as cash lose value? Cash in this calculator earns 0%, so prices rise each year while the balance stays the same. At 3% inflation, cash has a real return of -2.91% a year. Over 10 years, $10,000 held as cash buys what $7,441 buys today. That is 25.6% less buying power. How long does it take for inflation to halve my buying power? At 3% inflation, buying power halves in about 23.4 years. The calculator finds this with ln 2 / ln(1 + inflation). Does this calculator use historical CPI data? Yes, the "From a past year" mode uses historical Consumer Price Index (CPI) data. It pulls from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) , U.S. city average, all items, series CUUR0000SA0. You can pick any year from 1913 to 2025, and the latest month in the data is September 2026. The default future-cost mode still uses the rate you enter and has no forecast built in. Can I use this for retirement planning? It covers one part of retirement planning. The calculator shows how a fixed amount loses buying power over a retirement-length horizon at the rate you enter, and the optional return shows the ending balance in today's dollars. It does not model taxes, fees, withdrawals, or a rate that changes over time. For a full projection, use the retirement planning pages . Enter your child's age, the seed amount, and the annual contributions from your family and any employer in the calculator above to see the projected value. For example, a newborn's $1,000 seed, plus $200 a month at a 7% annual return, grows to about $89,657 by age 18: $44,200 put in and $45,457 in tax-deferred growth. Assumes one fixed return compounded monthly; real S&P 500 returns vary year to year. Trump Account funds must be invested in a U.S.-equity index fund and grow tax-deferred until 18. Further reading for the parent of a future account holder Make Your Kid a Money Genius (Even If You're Not) by Beth Kobliner Age-by-age money lessons, so your child is ready to manage this balance at 18. Check price on Amazon The Little Book of Common Sense Investing by John C. Bogle The index-fund logic behind the U.S.-equity fund this account must hold. Check price on Amazon Money for Couples by Ramit Sethi Helps two parents agree on how much to put in each year. Check price on Amazon As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. How it works The calculator above starts with the seed deposit, adds your yearly contributions in monthly steps, and compounds the balance at the return you choose until the child turns 18. Trump Accounts launched on July 4, 2026: the federal government seeds $1,000 for each U.S.-citizen child born between 2025 and 2028, and the money must be invested in a low-cost fund that tracks the S&P 500 or a similar U.S.-stock index. Growth is tax-deferred, and withdrawals are generally blocked until January 1 of the year the child turns 18 — after which the account is taxed like a traditional IRA. Contributions are capped. Families, relatives, and friends can add up to $5,000 per year combined, and an employer can chip in up to $2,500 — but that employer money counts toward the same $5,000 cap, not on top of it. The $1,000 federal seed does not count against the cap. Going over the cap has a real consequence beyond the calculator: contributing beyond the cap can trigger IRS correction requirements. The calculator mirrors that boundary by trimming anything you enter above the limits and showing a warning, so your projection reflects what the law actually allows. Time does the heavy lifting. The $1,000 seed alone, left untouched at a 7% return, grows to about $3,513 by age 18. Add $200 a month and the balance reaches roughly $89,657. Max out the $5,000 yearly limit from birth and it grows to about $182,980 — of which about half is growth you never contributed. This calculator only projects out to age 18, since that's when the account unlocks. For a longer horizon, like what $1,000 could grow into over 20 years, use the compound interest calculator instead. To compare that path against other accounts, see Trump Account vs 529 , Trump Account vs a custodial account , Trump Account vs a savings account , Trump Account vs a brokerage account , Trump Account vs a Roth IRA , and Trump Account vs baby bonds , or read what a Trump Account is and how to open one . For step-by-step setup see how to open a Trump Account , the full contribution rules , and what the account is invested in . To pressure-test whether it's the right home for your money, see are Trump Accounts worth it . For a general projection with different assumptions, the investment calculator uses the same compounding math. Frequently asked questions How does this Trump Account calculator work? The Trump Account calculator takes your child's age, the $1,000 federal seed, and your yearly family and employer contributions, then compounds the balance monthly at the return you choose until age 18. It enforces the $5,000 yearly contribution cap (including the $2,500 employer limit) so the projection matches the real rules. The result is an estimate — actual index returns vary year to year, and the projection does not model any account fees. Our Trump Account worth-it guide covers what, if anything, the account costs. How much will a Trump Account be worth at 18? It depends on contributions and returns. The $1,000 seed alone at a 7% average return grows to about $3,513 by age 18. Adding $200 a month brings it to roughly $89,657, and contributing the full $5,000 per year from birth reaches about $182,980. Use the calculator above to model your own numbers. Because the account is invested in a stock index, the balance can also fall in a bad year rather than just grow more slowly. See our Trump Account vs brokerage account comparison for how large a real downturn has gotten. Who gets the $1,000 Trump Account seed? The federal government deposits $1,000 for each U.S.-citizen child born between January 1, 2025 and December 31, 2028 who has a Social Security number. Children outside that birth window can still have a Trump Account opened and funded, but they do not receive the $1,000 seed. Set the seed to $0 in the calculator if your child isn't eligible. How much can you contribute to a Trump Account each year? Up to $5,000 per year combined from family, relatives, and friends. An employer can contribute up to $2,500, but that amount counts toward the same $5,000 cap rather than adding to it. The $1,000 federal seed is separate and does not count against the limit. The cap is indexed to inflation after 2027, so our Trump savings account guide is where to check the current-year number before assuming last year's cap still applies. Is Trump Account growth taxed? Growth inside a Trump Account is tax-deferred — you owe no tax on gains while the money stays invested. Contributions are made with after-tax dollars and are not deductible. Once the child turns 18, the account is treated like a traditional IRA, so withdrawals are generally taxed as income. Compare the tax treatment in our Trump Account vs 529 guide. Who manages a Trump Account before the child turns 18? A parent or legal guardian opens the account and manages it on the child's behalf until then; the money legally belongs to the child, not the parent. At 18, the child gains full control and the account starts working like a traditional IRA. A parent's immigration status does not affect a child's eligibility; see the full eligibility rules for details. Is TrumpAccounts.gov legit, or is it a scam? TrumpAccounts.gov is the real, official U.S. Treasury site for opening a Trump Account, live since the program's July 4, 2026 launch. Copycat sites, phishing texts, and fake "processing fee" calls have already shown up around the program; see Trump Account scams to know for the full list of red flags before you enter your child's Social Security number anywhere. Does an adopted child qualify for a Trump Account the same as a biological child? Yes, an adopted child qualifies for a Trump Account the same way a biological child does. The law's eligibility test looks only at citizenship, birth year, and having a Social Security number. If the adoption finalizes after the child's 2025-2028 birth window, confirm the exact timing rule on the IRS's Trump Accounts page before assuming either way. Provisional income is half your Social Security benefits plus all your other income and any tax-exempt interest. Above $25,000 (single) or $32,000 (married filing jointly), up to 50% of benefits is taxable. Above $34,000 or $44,000, up to 85% is taxable. The Social Security taxable benefits calculator below returns the taxable part, your provisional income, the share of benefits taxed and which tier applies. How it works The calculator follows Worksheet 1 of Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Publication 915 and starts with provisional income. Provisional income is all your other income plus tax-exempt interest plus half your benefits. Other income covers pensions, individual retirement account (IRA) withdrawals, wages, interest and dividends. For benefits, enter box 5 of your Social Security Administration (SSA) statement, Form SSA-1099, with both spouses' benefits on a joint return, or 12 times your monthly benefit before Medicare. Tax-exempt interest from municipal bonds counts too. Adding $5,000 of it to the joint example below raises provisional income to $56,000. Taxable benefits then go from $11,950 to $16,200, or 38.6% of the benefits. The calculator compares provisional income with a base amount and an upper amount for your filing status. The base amount is $25,000 if you are single, head of household, a qualifying surviving spouse, or married filing separately and lived apart all year. It is $32,000 for married filing jointly and $0 for married filing separately if you lived with your spouse at any time in the year. At or below the base amount, none of your benefits is taxable. Between the base amount and $34,000 ($44,000 joint), the taxable part is the smaller of half the benefits or half the income above the base. Above $34,000 ($44,000 joint), the taxable part is the smaller of 85% of the benefits or a second figure. That second figure is 85% of the income above the upper amount, plus the smaller of half the benefits or $4,500 ($6,000 joint). Take the joint couple with $42,000 of benefits and $30,000 of other income. Half the benefits is $21,000, so provisional income is $51,000. That is above the $44,000 joint upper amount, so the 85% tier applies. The income above $44,000 is $7,000. Taking 85% of that gives $5,950. The smaller of half the benefits or $6,000 is $6,000, and adding it brings the total to $11,950. That total is under the cap of 85% of benefits, or $35,700, so $11,950 is taxable. The base and upper amounts are written into Title 26 of the United States Code, section 86, and are not indexed to inflation. Benefits rise with each cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) while those thresholds stay fixed, so a raise can push provisional income over a threshold and make more of your benefits taxable. Run your new benefit through the 2027 COLA calculator , then enter the yearly amount here. This calculator covers federal tax only, and the states that tax Social Security guide covers state rules. The deduction for people 65 and older is also separate. It is worth up to $6,000 per person for tax years 2025 through 2028. It lowers taxable income but does not change how much of your benefits counts as taxable, as the senior deduction guide explains. The calculator stops at the taxable amount and does not compute the tax you owe on it. If you want your total federal tax bill, this result is only the first step. The taxable part is added to your other income and taxed at your normal rates, and the tax bracket calculator shows the rate on that amount. Married filing separately while living with your spouse has a $0 base amount, so benefits are taxable from the first dollar of provisional income. The calculator leaves out worksheet adjustments such as student loan interest, the foreign earned income exclusion and lump-sum back payments for earlier years. For returns with those items, the IRS worksheet in tax software gives the exact figure. For the full background, read is Social Security taxable , then enter your own figures in the Social Security taxable benefits calculator above. Frequently asked questions How do I figure the taxable amount of Social Security benefits? Add half your benefits to all your other income and any tax-exempt interest to get provisional income. Above $25,000 single or $32,000 joint, up to 50% of benefits is taxable. Above $34,000 or $44,000, up to 85% is taxable. A joint couple with $42,000 of benefits and $30,000 of other income has $11,950 taxable. How do I calculate my taxable Social Security benefits for 2026? The calculator uses the method in the 2025 edition of IRS Publication 915. Its dollar thresholds come from the tax code and are not indexed to inflation. Enter your benefits from box 5 of Form SSA-1099, or 12 times your monthly benefit before Medicare, along with your other income and tax-exempt interest. The calculator returns the taxable part and the share of benefits taxed. What is the formula for calculating the Social Security tax deduction? By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated October 28, 2026 Set aside 20% to 25% of your net profit if freelancing is your only income, and 30% to 35% if you also have a W-2 job — then add your state's income tax rate. The single figure everyone repeats, 30%, is too high for most full-time freelancers and too low for most side hustlers. On $45,000 of net profit with no other income, a single filer owes $8,579.50 in federal tax — 19.1%. Move the same $45,000 alongside a salary and the right figure changes completely. Share Interactive — edit any field How much to set aside Add your W-2 wages to see the real rate for side income Net profit (business income minus expenses) $ Filing status Single Married Head of hh W-2 wages from a job (if any) $ Wages use up the Social Security wage base first, so a day job lowers the Social Security part of your self-employment tax — but raises the income-tax rate your 1099 profit stacks on top of. Other household income $ Apply the 20% qualified business income (QBI) deduction Set aside from every payment 19.1% $8,580 of federal tax on $45,000 of net profit Self-employment tax $6,358 Federal income tax (on this income) $2,221 Quarterly payment (1040-ES) $2,145 Effective SE rate on profit 14.13% 2026 estimated tax due dates (Form 1040-ES) April 15, 2026 June 15, 2026 Sept. 15, 2026 Jan. 15, 2027 (next) A date on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day. You can skip the January payment if you file by February 1, 2027 and pay the full balance. For the safe-harbor amount that avoids the underpayment penalty, use the quarterly estimated tax calculator . Net earnings ($45,000 × 92.35%) $41,558 Social Security 12.4% on $41,558 $5,153 Medicare 2.9% (no ceiling) $1,205 Deduction for half of SE tax − $3,179 QBI deduction (20%) − $5,144 Estimate only, using 2026 federal figures: a $184,500 Social Security wage base and the Rev. Proc. 2025-32 brackets and standard deduction. It does not include state or local income tax, a self-employed health insurance or retirement deduction, or tax credits. Further reading on taxes when you work for yourself Independent Contractor, Sole Proprietor, and LLC Taxes Explained in 100 Pages or Less by Mike Piper Self-employment tax, quarterly payments and deductions in one short read. Check price on Amazon Working for Yourself: Law & Taxes for Independent Contractors by Stephen Fishman (Nolo) The law and tax rules that come with working for yourself. Check price on Amazon Deduct It! Lower Your Small Business Taxes by Stephen Fishman (Nolo) Deductions that lower the profit this percentage applies to. Check price on Amazon J.K. Lasser's Your Income Tax 2027 (for preparing your 2026 return) A full guide for filing this year's return. Check price on Amazon As an Amazon Associate we earn from qualifying purchases. How it's calculated The set-aside percentage is not one number because two different taxes stack in different ways. Self-employment tax is the flat part. It is 15.3% of 92.35% of profit, an effective 14.13%, and it applies from the very first dollar of profit up to the $184,500 Social Security wage base. Nothing shelters it — not the standard deduction, not the QBI deduction. If you set aside nothing else, set aside this. Federal income tax is the variable part, and it is where the flat rules of thumb break. It applies only to what is left after half your self-employment tax, the standard deduction, and the QBI deduction come off. For a single filer with no other income, that means income tax is zero until profit reaches roughly $17,400. Between there and $50,000 it climbs slowly. A part-time freelancer earning $15,000 of profit needs 14.1%, not 30% — setting aside 30% would idle more than a thousand dollars for a year. The direction reverses the moment you have a job. Your salary fills the low brackets first, so every dollar of freelance profit is taxed at your top marginal rate. Your W-2 withholding already covers your salary, so what you must fund yourself is only the extra tax the freelance income causes. Earn $80,000 at a job and $20,000 freelancing, and that extra tax is $6,097.23 on the $20,000 — 30.5%. The same $20,000 earned by someone with no job would cost 14.1%. That is the calculation the tool above performs, and it is the reason its headline is a percentage rather than a bill. It computes your household tax with the self-employment income and without it, and reports the difference against your profit. Two adjustments are yours to make. State income tax is not modelled here and ranges from zero to over 10%. And if your income is lumpy, set aside from every payment as it arrives rather than saving a quarterly lump — a percentage moved on the day money clears survives a slow month in a way a good intention does not. Where the money goes matters less than that it leaves your spending account. A separate high-yield savings account is enough. Our guide to budgeting with irregular income covers the quarterly due dates and the safe-harbour rule, and the 1099 tax calculator shows the full breakdown behind the percentage. A worked example Two people each earn $20,000 of freelance profit in 2026. The first has no other income: their self-employment tax is $2,825.91, the standard deduction wipes out nearly all their income tax, and their total federal bill is $3,024.87 — a 15.1% set-aside. The second already earns $80,000 in a salaried job. Their self-employment tax on the same $20,000 is identical at $2,825.91, but the profit stacks on top of their salary in the 22% bracket, so the freelance income adds $6,097.23 to the household bill once income tax is counted. That is a 30.5% set-aside on the same $20,000 of work — double the first person's rate, for identical income. Common mistakes to avoid Applying 30% to everything. It over-saves for a full-time freelancer under $50,000 of profit and under-saves for almost anyone with a day job. Setting aside a share of gross invoices rather than profit. If you have real expenses, the percentage applies to what is left after them — otherwise you are saving against money you already spent on the business. Forgetting state income tax. Every percentage here is federal. In a high-tax state the real figure can be five to ten points higher. Waiting to save until the quarterly due date. Income that arrives unevenly gets spent unevenly; moving the percentage the day each payment clears is what makes the quarterly payment possible. Ignoring the effect of a spouse's income. On a joint return your profit stacks on the household total, which can push the set-aside rate several points higher than a single-earner estimate. Frequently asked questions Should I set aside 30% for 1099 taxes? Only if you also have a W-2 job or earn well into six figures. For a full-time freelancer with no other income, 20% to 25% of net profit covers federal tax at typical earnings, and under about $17,400 of profit the real figure is just the 14.1% self-employment tax. With a day job, 30% to 35% is right, because freelance income is taxed at your top marginal rate on top of your salary. Add state tax to any of these. Do I set aside a percentage of gross income or profit? Profit — gross income minus business expenses. Tax is calculated on Schedule C net profit, so saving a percentage of gross over-saves by exactly your expense ratio. The practical method is to estimate your expenses as a share of revenue, then apply the set-aside percentage to the remainder of each payment as it arrives. Where should I keep money set aside for taxes? A separate savings account that is not your spending account, ideally one paying interest. The point is friction: money in your checking account gets spent, and the quarterly payment then has to come out of next month's income. Some freelancers use a dedicated business savings account and transfer the set-aside percentage the day each client payment clears. How much should I set aside if my income varies every month? Set aside a fixed percentage of every payment rather than a fixed dollar amount per month. A percentage self-adjusts: a big month contributes more, a lean month contributes less, and you never have to predict the year in advance. Recheck the percentage mid-year — if income has run well above or below plan, the right rate has moved with it. What if I set aside too much? You get it back, either as a refund or as a smaller final quarterly payment. Over-saving costs you only the interest on the surplus, which is why erring high is the safer mistake. Under-saving costs you the shortfall plus a possible underpayment penalty, at a moment when the money has already been spent. How it's calculated Estimated tax covers both halves of what you owe: self-employment tax and federal income tax on your profit. The calculator above works out the annual figure and divides it into four, which is the right starting point for income that arrives evenly. The payments are due four times a year — in April, June, and September, and again in January of the following year. The instalments are not quarters of equal length, which surprises people: the second period covers only two months. Payments are made through IRS Direct Pay, EFTPS, or with a mailed 1040-ES voucher. The safe harbor is the part worth understanding properly, because it converts an uncertain obligation into a fixed one. You avoid the underpayment penalty if you pay at least 90% of the current year's total tax, or 100% of last year's total tax — 110% if your prior-year adjusted gross income was over $150,000. The prior-year route is the one most self-employed people should use, because last year's number is already known and this year's is a forecast. Pay the prior-year amount in four instalments and the penalty is switched off regardless of how much better the year turns out to be. If your income is genuinely lumpy, there is a second option: the annualised income instalment method, which lets you pay in proportion to what you actually earned in each period rather than in four equal amounts. It requires more record-keeping and Form 2210 Schedule AI at filing time, but it prevents the situation where a strong fourth quarter creates a penalty for the first three. Two practical notes. If you also have a W-2 job, increasing withholding there is often easier than making estimated payments, and withholding is treated as paid evenly across the year regardless of when it actually happened — which can retroactively fix an underpayment that estimated payments cannot. And most states with an income tax run their own estimated payment system with separate deadlines and penalties. The reliable habit is to move a percentage of every payment into a separate account as it arrives, rather than trying to find a lump sum four times a year. Our guide to how much to set aside works out the percentage, and the guide to budgeting with irregular income covers the cash-flow side. A worked example A freelancer with $60,000 of net profit and no other income owes $8,478 of self-employment tax and $3,559 of federal income tax — $12,037 for the year, or $3,009 per instalment. Suppose their prior-year total federal tax was $9,800 and their prior-year AGI was under $150,000. Paying four instalments of $2,450 — 100% of last year's tax — switches off the underpayment penalty even though the real liability is $12,037. They will owe the $2,237 difference at filing, but without a penalty, and the certainty is usually worth more than the deferral. Common mistakes to avoid Assuming the payment periods are equal quarters. The second period covers only two months, so a literal quarterly rhythm misses a deadline. Estimating this year's income instead of using the prior-year safe harbor. Last year's figure is already known and switches off the penalty regardless of how this year turns out. Forgetting the 110% rule. If your prior-year AGI was over $150,000, the safe harbor is 110% of last year's tax rather than 100%. Paying the whole balance in April. The penalty is for not paying as you go, so it can apply even when you pay in full at filing. Ignoring state estimated payments. Most states with an income tax run their own system with separate deadlines and separate penalties. Frequently asked questions When are quarterly estimated taxes due? Four times a year: in April, June, and September, and again in January of the following year. The periods are not equal quarters — the second covers only two months — so a strict three-month rhythm will miss a deadline. Payments can be made through IRS Direct Pay, EFTPS, or by mailing a Form 1040-ES voucher. What is the safe harbor rule for estimated taxes? You avoid the underpayment penalty by paying at least 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's total tax, rising to 110% if your prior-year adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000. The prior-year route is the practical choice for self-employed filers, because it relies on a number you already know rather than a forecast of a year still in progress. What happens if I don't pay quarterly taxes? An underpayment penalty can apply even if you pay the full balance when you file, because the rule is about paying as you go rather than paying in total. The penalty is calculated per period, so missing early instalments costs more than missing the last one. Meeting a safe harbor removes the penalty regardless of the final balance owed. Can I pay estimated taxes through payroll withholding instead? Yes, if you also have a W-2 job, and it is often easier. Withholding is treated as paid evenly throughout the year no matter when it actually occurred, so increasing it late in the year can retroactively cure an underpayment that estimated payments cannot. Ask your employer to adjust your Form W-4 to withhold an additional amount each pay period. What if my income varies a lot between quarters? Use the annualised income instalment method, which lets you pay in proportion to what you actually earned in each period instead of in four equal amounts. It requires tracking income by period and completing Schedule AI of Form 2210 at filing, but it prevents a strong final quarter from creating penalties for the earlier ones. The prior-year safe harbor is the simpler alternative if you can fund it. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. Enter your current balance, interest rate, months left and lump sum in the mortgage recast calculator below, along with any recast fee your servicer charges. The calculator returns the new payment, the interest saved and the months a fee takes to earn back, and it also shows the same lump sum prepaid without a recast. For example, take a $238,000 balance at 6.875% with 312 months left. The payment is $1,639.33 a month in principal and interest. A $30,000 recast cuts it to $1,432.69, which is $206.64 a month less. Not every loan can be recast: your servicer decides, and many do not recast government-backed loans such as FHA and VA loans. How it works The mortgage recast calculator sets a payment with payment = balance × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the annual rate divided by 12 and n is the months left. A recast reruns the formula on the lower balance with the same r and n. On the example loan, the new $208,000 balance gives a payment of $1,432.69, down from $1,639.33. Enter the recast fee your servicer charges, and the calculator shows how many months of the lower payment it takes to earn the fee back. On the example, a $250 fee is earned back in 2 months, and the recast still saves $34,221.26 in interest after the fee. Prepay $30,000 without a recast and keep paying $1,639.33, and the lower balance clears the example loan in 228 months. That is 84 months, or 7 years, sooner, with $109,002.12 saved in interest. The recast saves $34,471.26, so it gives up interest savings in exchange for a lower required payment. A recast fits a borrower who wants a lower required payment, for example after a home sale or a drop in income. If you want to shorten the loan, prepay without a recast and use the mortgage payoff calculator to test monthly extra payments. To compare paying down the mortgage with investing the lump sum, read the pay off mortgage early or invest guide. The calculator assumes a fixed-rate loan and shows principal and interest only, so taxes and insurance are not included. Your servicer sets the recast fee and the minimum lump sum. The servicer also decides whether a loan can be recast at all. Your servicer may charge a recast fee, and it may not recast your loan at all. What are the benefits of recasting? A recast lowers your required monthly payment and keeps the same rate and months left. On the example loan, a $30,000 lump sum lowers the payment by $206.64 a month. It also saves $34,471.26 in interest over the remaining 312 months. Is it better to recast or just pay extra principal? Paying extra principal without a recast saves more interest, and a recast gives a lower required payment. With the same $30,000, prepaying ends the example loan 84 months sooner and saves $109,002.12. The recast saves $34,471.26 but cuts the payment by $206.64 a month. You can create one in Excel or Google Sheets using two formulas: one to calculate your fixed monthly payment and another to divide each payment between interest and principal. This walkthrough takes you through both formulas cell by cell, using a $400,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years as the running example. Swap in your own numbers, and the entire schedule will recalculate. There's no downloadable file here because every loan has a different balance, rate, and term. By entering the formulas yourself, you can make sure the schedule matches your exact loan. Prefer to skip the spreadsheet entirely? Our free mortgage amortization schedule calculator runs the same math instantly. Tools for this journey Amortization schedule → Mortgage payoff → Mortgage calculator → What the Amortization Formula Actually Does A fixed-rate loan charges interest only on the balance you still owe, so the payment splits differently every month even though the dollar amount never changes. Interest dominates the early payments, because the balance is largest right after closing. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) explains it plainly: lenders use a standard formula so a fixed payment retires the loan exactly at the end of the term, with the interest-to-principal ratio drifting the entire way. Three numbers drive that formula: the loan amount, the interest rate, and the term in months. Change any one of them and the entire schedule shifts underneath you. That is the whole mechanism behind mortgage amortization , and it is exactly what the next three steps rebuild in a spreadsheet. This same formula also reveals the total interest you will pay over the life of the loan. On the $400,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years, 360 payments of about $2,528 add up to roughly $910,080 paid in total. Subtract the $400,000 you borrowed, and interest alone accounts for about $510,000 of that. Seeing that figure spelled out often pushes a reader to look seriously at a shorter term or an extra-payment plan. Step 1: Calculate the Fixed Monthly Payment Open a blank sheet and label five input cells: loan amount, annual rate, term in years, monthly rate, and total payments. Put your loan amount in B1 (400000 for the example), your annual rate in B2 as a decimal (0.065 for 6.5%), and your term in years in B3 (30). In B4, find the monthly rate with =B2/12. In B5, find the total number of payments with =B3*12. In B6, calculate the fixed payment with the built-in PMT function : =PMT(B4,B5,-B1). The negative sign on the loan amount is required, since PMT returns a negative number without it. For the $400,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years, B6 returns roughly $2,528. That single number is the payment every row of your schedule references. Step 2: Split Each Payment into Interest and Principal Build a new table with six headers across row 1: Month, Starting Balance, Payment, Interest, Principal, Ending Balance. In row 2, enter 1 for Month and =$B$1 for Starting Balance, so it pulls your loan amount. For Payment, reference the fixed payment you already calculated: =$B$6. For Interest, multiply that row's starting balance by the monthly rate: =C2*$B$4. For Principal, subtract interest from the payment: =D2-E2. For Ending Balance, subtract principal from the starting balance: =C2-F2. Excel and Google Sheets also offer IPMT and PPMT functions that calculate this same split in one cell each, if you would rather skip the manual subtraction. Step 3: Copy the Formula Down the Full Schedule In row 3, set Month to 2 and Starting Balance to the prior row's Ending Balance: =G2. Select the formulas in row 3 and drag the fill handle down through row 361, since a 30-year loan runs 360 monthly payments. Your final row's Ending Balance should land at or extremely close to zero. That confirms the schedule pays the loan off exactly on schedule. The payment formula is built to guarantee exactly that. Add a running-total column with =SUM($E$2:E2) copied down every row if you want to see cumulative interest paid at any point in the loan. That column answers a question the payment figure alone never does: how much interest a specific payoff date actually costs you. Common Mistakes That Break the Schedule We see one mistake most often when readers build this formula themselves: using the annual rate instead of the monthly rate in the interest calculation. That single swap inflates every interest figure by roughly 12 times, and it is the most common error in a homemade schedule. Two other errors show up almost as often. Forgetting to lock a reference with a dollar sign, such as $B$4, lets the formula drift as you copy it down hundreds of rows. Rounding the payment to the nearest dollar early creates a small mismatch that compounds into a real gap by the final row. Reconcile your work against the built-in CUMIPMT function , which totals interest over a range of payments without a row-by-row table. If your running total and CUMIPMT disagree by more than a few dollars, check the rate and reference cells first. When the Live Calculator Beats a Spreadsheet A spreadsheet is the right tool for understanding exactly how the math works, and for a loan that never changes. It is the wrong tool once you want to test an extra $200 a month toward principal, compare a 15-year term against a 30-year term, or see how a refinance offer changes your total interest, since each scenario means rebuilding rows by hand. Our free mortgage amortization schedule calculator runs this same formula instantly and lets you test extra payments and different terms without touching a single cell reference. If you are deciding whether an extra payment plan is worth it in the first place, the mortgage payoff calculator shows the years and interest it would save. Build the spreadsheet once to understand the mechanism. Reach for the calculator every time after that. Frequently asked questions What is the mortgage amortization formula? The fixed monthly payment formula is M = P times [r(1+r)^n] divided by [(1+r)^n minus 1], where P is the loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate, and n is the total number of payments. Excel and Google Sheets calculate the same result with the built-in PMT function: =PMT(rate, nper, -pv). How do I calculate a mortgage payment in Excel? Enter your monthly rate, total number of payments, and loan amount, then use =PMT(monthly_rate, total_payments, -loan_amount). The negative sign on the loan amount is required for the function to return a positive payment. How much of my first mortgage payment goes to interest? Most of it. On a $400,000 loan at 6.5% over 30 years, the first payment of about $2,528 includes roughly $2,167 in interest and only $361 in principal, because interest is calculated on the full starting balance. Does the amortization formula change for a 15-year loan instead of a 30-year loan? The formula stays the same. Only the term input changes, from 360 monthly payments to 180. A shorter term produces a higher monthly payment, but a much smaller share of each payment goes to interest, since the balance shrinks faster. Can I model extra principal payments in this spreadsheet? Yes, by adding an Extra Payment column and subtracting it from the Ending Balance formula each month, though the schedule then runs fewer than 360 rows and needs a formula that stops once the balance hits zero. Our mortgage payoff calculator models extra payments without any spreadsheet work. Is there a downloadable amortization schedule file I can just open? No. This guide teaches the formulas so you can build a schedule for your own exact loan amount, rate, and term, since a generic downloadable file would not match your numbers. Prefer not to build one? The free mortgage amortization schedule calculator generates your full schedule instantly online. Does this formula work for an adjustable-rate mortgage? Only between rate changes. An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) uses this exact formula for each fixed-rate period, but once the rate resets, you have to recalculate the payment using the loan's remaining balance, the new rate, and the remaining term as new inputs. A fixed-rate loan never needs that recalculation, which is one reason the formula is easiest to learn on a fixed-rate example first. Does a biweekly payment schedule use the same formula? Not directly. Paying half your monthly payment every two weeks results in 26 half-payments a year, the equivalent of 13 full monthly payments instead of 12, which this formula does not account for on its own. Our biweekly mortgage calculator models a biweekly schedule and the extra payment it effectively adds each year. Self-Employment Tax calculators 1099 Tax Calculator Free · instant How Much Should I Set Aside For Taxes 1099 Free · instant DoorDash Taxes Free · instant Uber Driver Taxes Free · instant Uber Eats Taxes Free · instant Lyft Driver Taxes Free · instant Instacart Taxes Free · instant Amazon Flex Taxes Free · instant Shipt Taxes Free · instant Rover Taxes Free · instant Twitch Taxes Free · instant Upwork Taxes Free · instant Fiverr Taxes Free · instant Etsy Seller Taxes Free · instant DataAnnotation Taxes Free · instant YouTube Taxes Free · instant Quarterly Estimated Tax Calculator Free · instant How it works Self-employment tax replaces the Social Security and Medicare taxes an employer would otherwise split with you. A W-2 employee pays 7.65% and the employer pays the matching 7.65%. When you work for yourself you are both parties, so you pay the full 15.3%. The rate is not applied to your full profit. Schedule SE first multiplies net profit by 92.35%, which approximates the employer half an employee would never have been taxed on. That step is why the effective rate on profit is 14.13%, not 15.3% — and why a calculator that skips it overstates your bill by about 8%. The two halves behave differently above a threshold. The 12.4% Social Security portion stops once your combined wages and net earnings reach the wage base, which is $184,500 for 2026. The 2.9% Medicare portion never stops, and an extra 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies above $200,000 ($250,000 for joint filers). If you also hold a W-2 job, those wages consume the Social Security wage base first, so a moonlighter with a high salary can owe far less Social Security tax on their side income than the raw 15.3% suggests. One deduction comes back to you automatically: half of your self-employment tax is an above-the-line deduction against income tax. The calculator applies it, and it excludes the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax, which is not deductible. The set-aside share shown above is deliberately not your household tax bill divided by your profit. If you have a day job, your W-2 withholding already covers the tax on that salary. What you have to fund yourself is the extra tax your self-employment income causes on top of it. That number is often higher than freelancers expect: a side hustle stacks on top of your salary, so it is taxed at your top marginal rate from the first dollar. Someone earning $80,000 at a job plus $20,000 on the side sets aside about 30.5% of the side income, while a full-time freelancer earning $45,000 sets aside about 19.1%. You pay this as you go, not in April. The IRS expects quarterly estimated payments via Form 1040-ES, and there is a penalty for underpaying even if you settle up in full at filing. Our guide to budgeting with irregular income covers the four due dates and the safe-harbor rules that make the penalty go away. Frequently asked questions How much is self-employment tax in 2026? Self-employment tax is 15.3% of net earnings: 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. Because it applies to 92.35% of your net profit rather than all of it, the effective rate on profit is 14.13%. The Social Security portion stops at $184,500 of combined wages and net earnings in 2026; the Medicare portion has no ceiling, and an extra 0.9% applies above $200,000 ($250,000 married filing jointly). How much should I set aside for taxes as a 1099 contractor? For a full-time freelancer with no other income, 20% to 25% of net profit covers federal self-employment and income tax at typical earnings — $60,000 of profit produces about 20.1%. Set aside more if you have a W-2 job, because side income stacks on top of your salary and is taxed at your highest marginal rate: someone earning $80,000 at a job plus $20,000 freelancing needs about 30.5% of the freelance income. Add your state income tax rate on top of any of these figures. Why is self-employment tax calculated on 92.35% of my profit? Because a W-2 employee is never taxed on the employer's half of FICA, and Schedule SE approximates that treatment for the self-employed. Multiplying net profit by 92.35% removes roughly the employer-share equivalent before the 15.3% rate is applied. It is the reason your real rate is 14.13% of profit, and it happens automatically on Schedule SE — you do not have to elect it. Do I pay self-employment tax if I already pay Social Security at my job? You still pay the 2.9% Medicare portion, but your W-2 wages consume the Social Security wage base first. If your wages already reach $184,500 in 2026, no Social Security tax applies to your self-employment income at all — only Medicare. Below that, the 12.4% applies just to the remaining room under the wage base. Enter your W-2 wages in the calculator above and the breakdown shows exactly how much Social Security tax is left to pay. Do I owe self-employment tax if I made less than $2,000? Self-employment tax applies once your net earnings from self-employment reach $400 for the year — that threshold is unrelated to whether anyone sends you a tax form. For 2026 a payer only has to issue a Form 1099-NEC at $2,000 (raised from $600), and payment apps only issue a 1099-K above $20,000 and 200 transactions. The IRS is explicit that you report gig income "even if the income is... not reported on an information return form." No form does not mean no tax. Can I lower my self-employment tax? Only by lowering net profit, since the tax is charged on profit rather than revenue. Every legitimate business deduction — mileage, home office, software, equipment, supplies — cuts self-employment tax and income tax at the same time, which is why a deduction is worth far more to a 1099 earner than to an employee. Retirement contributions to a SEP-IRA or solo 401(k) reduce income tax but not self-employment tax. At higher profit levels, electing S-corporation treatment can reduce the base the 15.3% applies to, at the cost of running payroll. mainEntity.name: How much is self-employment tax in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Self-employment tax is 15.3% of net earnings: 12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare. Because it applies to 92.35% of your net profit rather than all of it, the effective rate on profit is 14.13%. The Social Security portion stops at $184,500 of combined wages and net earnings in 2026; the Medicare portion has no ceiling, and an extra 0.9% applies above $200,000 ($250,000 married filing jointly).

mainEntity.name: How much should I set aside for taxes as a 1099 contractor?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a full-time freelancer with no other income, 20% to 25% of net profit covers federal self-employment and income tax at typical earnings — $60,000 of profit produces about 20.1%. Set aside more if you have a W-2 job, because side income stacks on top of your salary and is taxed at your highest marginal rate: someone earning $80,000 at a job plus $20,000 freelancing needs about 30.5% of the freelance income. Add your state income tax rate on top of any of these figures.

mainEntity.name: Why is self-employment tax calculated on 92.35% of my profit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because a W-2 employee is never taxed on the employer's half of FICA, and Schedule SE approximates that treatment for the self-employed. Multiplying net profit by 92.35% removes roughly the employer-share equivalent before the 15.3% rate is applied. It is the reason your real rate is 14.13% of profit, and it happens automatically on Schedule SE — you do not have to elect it.

mainEntity.name: Do I pay self-employment tax if I already pay Social Security at my job?

acceptedAnswer.text: You still pay the 2.9% Medicare portion, but your W-2 wages consume the Social Security wage base first. If your wages already reach $184,500 in 2026, no Social Security tax applies to your self-employment income at all — only Medicare. Below that, the 12.4% applies just to the remaining room under the wage base. Enter your W-2 wages in the calculator above and the breakdown shows exactly how much Social Security tax is left to pay.

mainEntity.name: Do I owe self-employment tax if I made less than $2,000?

acceptedAnswer.text: Self-employment tax applies once your net earnings from self-employment reach $400 for the year — that threshold is unrelated to whether anyone sends you a tax form. For 2026 a payer only has to issue a Form 1099-NEC at $2,000 (raised from $600), and payment apps only issue a 1099-K above $20,000 and 200 transactions. The IRS is explicit that you report gig income "even if the income is... not reported on an information return form." No form does not mean no tax.

mainEntity.name: Can I lower my self-employment tax?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only by lowering net profit, since the tax is charged on profit rather than revenue. Every legitimate business deduction — mileage, home office, software, equipment, supplies — cuts self-employment tax and income tax at the same time, which is why a deduction is worth far more to a 1099 earner than to an employee. Retirement contributions to a SEP-IRA or solo 401(k) reduce income tax but not self-employment tax. At higher profit levels, electing S-corporation treatment can reduce the base the 15.3% applies to, at the cost of running payroll.
